Journal of Clinical Oncology

Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy Versus Surgical Resection for Early-Stage Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: An Emulated Target Trial

Kagenaar E, Lugo-Palacios DG, Aggarwal A et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Emulated target trial (observational registry-linked cohort with instrumental variable analysis), England, 2015-2020.
Key Question: Does SABR achieve survival outcomes comparable to surgical resection in early-stage (T1-2N0M0) NSCLC patients eligible for either treatment?
Key Findings:
  • 12,546 patients (2,299 SABR; 10,247 surgery). Adjusted 3-year all-cause mortality was 30.3% with SABR versus 21.6% with surgery (absolute difference 8.8 pp, 95% CI 1.4 to 16.2; P = .02).
  • Lung cancer-specific mortality difference was not significant (6.1 pp, 95% CI -0.6 to 12.9).
  • In patients aged 80+, the all-cause mortality difference was 4.3 pp (95% CI -3.7 to 12.3), with no significant difference detected.
Clinical Relevance: Using national English data, this supports surgery as preferred where patients are fit for either modality, while SABR remains a reasonable curative-intent option, particularly in older patients, to inform MDT discussions.
Limitations: Despite instrumental variable methods, residual confounding by indication cannot be excluded in a non-randomised design, and the subgroup analysis in older patients was likely underpowered.

European Journal of Cancer

Early discontinuation of immune checkpoint inhibitors after objective response in real-world melanoma: Clinical and economic impact

Jurlander RS, Borch TH, Petersen SK et al. · 2026 Oct 22
Study Type: Retrospective national registry cohort study (Danish Metastatic Melanoma Database), single-arm, no comparator.
Key Question: What are the long-term outcomes of elective ICI discontinuation (≤18 months) in advanced melanoma patients with a complete or partial response?
Key Findings:
  • 163 patients (82 CR, 81 PR) stopped first-line anti-PD1 ± anti-CTLA4 at a median of 8.1 months (CR) and 11.1 months (PR); median follow-up was 48 months.
  • 36-month PFS was 87% (CR) and 81% (PR); OS was 98% (CR) and 87% (PR).
  • 36-month melanoma-specific survival was 99% (CR) and 93% (PR). The authors report potential cost savings but the abstract gives no figures.
Clinical Relevance: Supports response-guided stopping before two years, which is relevant to NHS decisions on treatment duration, toxicity burden and drug expenditure.
Limitations: No comparator arm of patients continuing treatment, and the cohort is selected on survival to discontinuation (immortal time bias), so these data cannot show that early cessation is non-inferior to standard duration.

European Journal of Cancer

PELICAN-IPC 2015-016/Oncodistinct-003: A randomized non-comparative phase II study of pembrolizumab in combination with neoadjuvant chemotherapy in HER2-negative inflammatory breast cancer

de Nonneville A, Lerebours F, Zemmour C et al. · 2026 Oct 31
Study Type: Randomised, non-comparative, multicentre phase II trial.
Key Question: Does adding pembrolizumab to neoadjuvant EC-paclitaxel improve pathological response in HER2-negative inflammatory breast cancer (IBC)?
Key Findings:
  • Centrally assessed pCR in the pembrolizumab arm was 12.5% (4/32; 90% CI 4.4–26.4): 6.3% in ER-positive and 18.8% in triple-negative disease.
  • Chemotherapy-alone arm pCR was 35.0% (22.2% ER-positive; 45.5% triple-negative). This was numerically higher, though the trial was not designed for comparison.
  • Grade ≥3 adverse events were similar between arms (69.7% vs 65.0%). Immune-related toxicities were consistent with the known pembrolizumab profile. PD-L1, TILs and CTC-based biomarkers did not predict response.
Clinical Relevance: These data do not support adding pembrolizumab to anthracycline-taxane neoadjuvant therapy in HER2-negative IBC, relevant to UK clinicians who may extrapolate from KEYNOTE-522 in non-inflammatory TNBC.
Limitations: Very small sample (n=53) with a non-comparative design and a 1:2 allocation, so no conclusions about relative efficacy can be drawn.

JAMA Oncology

HB0025 With Chemotherapy for Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Phase 2 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial

Zhou F, Wang L, Bai J et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Phase 2, open-label, multicentre, non-randomised trial (13 Chinese hospitals; n=169 evaluable).
Key Question: What are the efficacy and safety of HB0025 (PD-L1/VEGF bispecific antibody) plus platinum chemotherapy as first-line treatment for driver-negative advanced NSCLC?
Key Findings:
  • Confirmed ORR at 20 mg/kg: 57.1% (95% CI 44.1–69.5) nonsquamous; 74.2% (61.5–84.5) squamous. ORR at 10 mg/kg was 36.4% and 68.2% respectively.
  • Median PFS 12.5 months (95% CI 10.2–16.6) nonsquamous; 14.8 months (11.3–NE) squamous. 12-month OS 75.8% and 85.5%.
  • Grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs in 66% (nonsquamous) and 61% (squamous), mainly haematological; immune-related AEs of any grade in ~25%.
Clinical Relevance: PD-(L)1/VEGF bispecifics are an emerging first-line class, but this agent is unavailable in the UK and these data do not alter current NHS practice.
Limitations: Non-randomised with no comparator arm, so efficacy cannot be benchmarked against standard chemo-immunotherapy; the squamous cohort was 93% male, and follow-up and generalisability beyond a Chinese population are limited.

The Lancet Oncology

Activity and safety of first-line pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel in triple-negative breast cancer: a single-arm, phase 1b/2 trial

Zhang J, Shi Y, Zhang Q et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Single-arm, multicentre, phase 1b/2 trial (10 Chinese sites)
Key Question: What are the safety and objective response rate of first-line pumitamig (PD-L1/VEGF-A bispecific antibody) plus nab-paclitaxel in advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)?
Key Findings:
  • Confirmed ORR was 73.8% (95% CI 58.0–86.1; 31/42; 1 complete response, 30 partial responses) at median follow-up of 35.2 months.
  • Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events included neutrophil count decreased (31%), white cell count decreased (26%), proteinuria (14%) and febrile neutropenia (12%); 21% had treatment-related serious adverse events (including retinal vein occlusion, macular oedema and pancreatitis); no treatment-related deaths.
  • Treatment-related adverse events led to discontinuation of one or both agents in 21% of patients.
Clinical Relevance: This early signal of activity for dual PD-L1/VEGF blockade with taxane chemotherapy in first-line TNBC is of interest given limited options beyond pembrolizumab-chemotherapy, but the drug is investigational and not available in the UK.
Limitations: Single-arm design with an all-Chinese, small cohort (n=42) and no comparator or survival endpoints reported, so benefit over standard chemoimmunotherapy cannot be inferred (PD-L1 status was also not reported in the abstract).

JAMA Oncology

Global Proposal for the TNM Staging System for Poorly Differentiated Thyroid Cancer

Shi X, Liu Q, Scholfield D et al. · 2026 Nov 06
Study Type: Multicentre international retrospective cohort study with external validation (SEER).
Key Question: Can a PDTC-specific TNM staging system improve prognostic stratification over TNM-8, which currently applies differentiated thyroid cancer criteria to PDTC?
Key Findings:
  • Level VII nodal metastasis had markedly worse 5-year OS (45.2%) than level VI (73.2%) or lateral neck disease (56.7%), prompting reclassification from N1a to N1c.
  • The proposed system shifted stage I from 44.4% to 24.6% and stage IV from 18.5% to 32.4% of the 1010-patient IATCCG cohort.
  • Discrimination improved over TNM-8 in the derivation cohort (C-statistic 0.74 vs 0.71; difference 0.03, 95% CI 0.01–0.04), but the SEER validation gain (0.76 vs 0.74) was not significant (difference 0.02, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.06).
Clinical Relevance: If adopted by AJCC/UICC, this would substantially alter risk stratification for PDTC, with likely implications for UK MDT staging, follow-up intensity and adjuvant decisions.
Limitations: Retrospective data spanning 1984–2026 across 91 centres, with modest incremental discrimination gain and unconfirmed benefit in external validation (small SEER cohort, n=170).

European Journal of Cancer

Cytokine release syndrome across three immunotherapy platforms: A real-world patient-level comparison of CAR T-cell, T-cell engager, and immune checkpoint inhibitor therapies

Wein L, Ertl C, Rejeski K et al. · 2026 Nov 01
Study Type: Retrospective registry analysis (SERIO registry; n=1765 patients)
Key Question: How do the incidence, timing, severity, management and associated toxicities of CRS differ between CAR-T, T-cell engager (tebentafusp/brenetafusp) and ICI therapy?
Key Findings:
  • CRS incidence: 88.7% (CAR-T), 63.3% (TCE), 0.7% (ICI). Grade ≥3 CRS: 11%, 4%, and 0% respectively. Median onset: 2.5 days, <1 day, and 21.5 days.
  • Tocilizumab use differed markedly (90% CAR-T vs 4% TCE vs 11% ICI). Concurrent toxicities differed by platform: ICANS (CAR-T), cutaneous (TCE), hepatitis/thyroiditis (ICI).
  • CRS resolved in 99–100%; one CRS-related death (CAR-T). No significant association between CRS and tumour response.
Clinical Relevance: Supports platform-specific CRS monitoring and management protocols rather than a uniform approach, relevant as TCEs expand in NHS practice.
Limitations: Only nine ICI-associated CRS cases and a TCE cohort limited to two agents restrict comparative inference; registry design risks reporting and selection bias.

European Journal of Cancer

Efficacy and safety of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy versus standard treatment in hemato-oncology: A systematic review and meta-analysis

Szilágyi Á, Varga P, Agócs G et al. · 2026 Nov 03
Study Type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (71 comparative studies; random-effects models)
Key Question: How does CAR T-cell therapy compare with standard non-CAR T treatments for efficacy and safety in NHL, ALL and multiple myeloma?
Key Findings:
  • NHL (mainly LBCL): CAR T improved response (OR 2.48, 95% CI 1.35–4.57) and OS (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.48–0.78) versus standard chemoimmunotherapy. PFS benefit was seen in second-line LBCL, but not versus targeted therapy or transplantation.
  • MM: PFS improved versus standard or targeted therapy (HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.11–0.77), with OS also favouring CAR T. ALL: OS favoured CAR T versus chemotherapy or DLI (HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.25–0.36).
  • Authors report no increase in overall toxicity; ALL showed fewer post-transplant GVHD events.
Clinical Relevance: Supports CAR T commissioning decisions in LBCL and myeloma, though benefit is comparator-dependent and no benefit was seen over transplantation or targeted therapy in some settings.
Limitations: Pooled non-randomised comparative studies (study mix not stated in the abstract) carry confounding and selection bias risks, and the abstract gives limited detail on heterogeneity or toxicity data.
